Chuffed means feeling very pleased, happy, or proud — usually because something good happened to you or you received a compliment, achieved something, or got some good news.

Think of it as that warm, glowing feeling you get when your hard work pays off, someone praises you sincerely, or things go better than you expected. It's not just mild happiness — it's the kind of pleased where you feel quietly proud and satisfied on the inside.

"Chuffed" is a bit richer than plain "happy." It almost always involves a personal stake — you're chuffed about something that matters to you, something you care about or worked for. It carries a small tinge of pride alongside the happiness. If someone says "I'm chuffed," they're not just smiling — they're beaming on the inside.

This is an informal British English word. It's everyday, casual language — the kind of word people use with friends, family, or colleagues in relaxed conversation, not in formal writing. It's also common in Australian and New Zealand English. If you're speaking to an American, they may not know this word, because it's rarely used in American English.

• "She was absolutely chuffed when her teacher praised her essay in front of the whole class."

→ She felt very proud and pleased.

  • "He got chuffed about winning the local football match."

→ He was really happy and proud about the win.

  • "I'm chuffed with how the dinner turned out — everyone loved it."

→ I'm pleased and satisfied with the result.

  • "They were chuffed to hear that their visa got approved."

→ They felt happy and relieved.

  • "She looked a bit chuffed with herself after the presentation."

→ She seemed quietly proud of herself.

Notice how in every case, the happiness is tied to something specific — an event, a result, a piece of praise, good news.
A phrase you'll often hear: "chuffed to bits"

This is an intensified version. "Chuffed to bits" means extremely pleased — completely over the moon about something.

  • "He was chuffed to bits when his daughter got into her dream university."
  • "I'm chuffed to bits with this new job offer!"

Think of "to bits" as adding emphasis, like saying "to pieces" — it ramps up the intensity of the feeling.
An important nuance to be aware of

Here is something slightly tricky, and worth knowing for accuracy: in some older dialects of Northern England (particularly Yorkshire), the word historically meant the opposite — displeased or annoyed. You may occasionally still come across this older usage in literature or in dialogue written by someone from that background. However, in standard modern British English, and in practically all everyday speech today, "chuffed" means pleased and happy — not annoyed. If you ever see it used to mean annoyed, it is almost certainly a regional or older usage, not the standard one.

• It doesn't mean excited in a buzzing, energetic way (that's more like "thrilled" or "pumped up"). Chuffed is warmer and calmer — more of a glow than a burst.
  • It doesn't mean relieved on its own, though you can certainly be chuffed about something that was also a relief.
  • It's not a strong emotion like ecstasy or euphoria — it's closer to deep, genuine contentment with a touch of pride.
